opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
When the readings are heard together, at first they seem like many separate ideas. But when you slow down, a single thread begins to appear. Each one is speaking about how God sees, how He leads, and how He brings a person into the light.
It begins with the moment when Samuel is sent to anoint a king in 1 Samuel 16:7. Samuel looks at the sons of Jesse and naturally assumes that the strongest and most impressive must be the one God has chosen. But the Lord corrects him:
“Not as man sees does God see, because man sees the appearance, but the Lord looks into the heart.”
Human beings are drawn to what is visible, measurable, and impressive. God sees something different. He looks into the heart. And the one God chooses is David, the shepherd boy, the one no one expected. From that moment forward, the Spirit of the Lord rushes upon him. The first theme becomes clear: God does not judge by outward appearance. He sees the heart.
The Psalm that follows helps explain what that looks like in the life of a person who allows God to lead. In Psalm 23 we hear the familiar words:
“The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.”
At first, this line can feel difficult, because the honest response is that we do want. Every person has desires, things they pursue, and things they believe will satisfy them. Yet the Psalm is not saying that a person will never feel desire. It is saying something deeper: if the Lord is truly the shepherd, then our wants no longer rule us.  The shepherd leads. The sheep follow. The Psalm describes a God who is constantly guiding and caring for the one who trusts Him—leading, restoring, protecting, and providing. At the center of the Psalm is the line:
“He guides me in right paths for His name’s sake.”
God is the one doing the leading. The second reading moves this idea into daily life. In Ephesians 5:10, Paul writes:
“Try to learn what is pleasing to the Lord.”
This is an important reminder that the Christian life is not about instant perfection. It is about learning. A gradual awakening. Paul then says:
“Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will give you light.” — Ephesians 5:14
There is a movement here: from sleep, to waking, to light. The Gospel then shows what that awakening looks like. In John 9, Jesus heals a man who has been blind since birth. The disciples immediately ask:
“Who sinned, this man or his parents?”
They assume suffering must be the result of sin. But Jesus answers:
“Neither he nor his parents sinned; it is so that the works of God might be made visible through him.” — John 9:3
At first the story seems to be about physical blindness. But as the story unfolds something deeper becomes clear. The blind man cannot see physically, yet the religious leaders—who believe they see perfectly—cannot see spiritually. By the end of the story, the one who was blind comes to see, while the leaders who believe they understand everything refuse to recognize what is happening before them. Jesus then says:
“I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see might see, and those who think they see might become blind.” — John 9:39
This reveals the thread that runs through all of the readings. They are all speaking about vision, but not eyesight—spiritual sight. Samuel shows that God sees the heart rather than outward appearance. The Psalm shows the Shepherd guiding the heart. Paul calls people to wake up and walk in the light. And in the Gospel, Jesus opens true sight. The real blindness in the Gospel is not physical blindness. It is the blindness of believing that we already see everything clearly. That is why Jesus says:
“If you were blind, you would have no sin. But now you say, ‘We see,’ so your sin remains.” — John 9:41
This is where the struggle about wanting things enters the picture. When we hear the words, “The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want,” the honest response can be: But I do want.  That honesty is not failure. In many ways it is the beginning of awakening. The danger is not that we have desires. The danger is allowing those desires to become our shepherd. Psalm 23 is not saying that a person will never have wants. It is saying that God becomes the one who leads them. A simple question can help reveal the line: Is this leading me closer to God, or replacing Him?  That question does not answer everything perfectly, but it exposes the direction of the heart. That is what Paul meant when he wrote, “Try to learn what is pleasing to the Lord.” Even the saints had to learn that slowly. At the center of all the readings stands the voice of Christ:
“I am the light of the world.” — John 9:5
Paul says, “Awake, O sleeper.”  The Psalm says, “He guides me.” Samuel reminds us that God sees the heart. All of them together are pointing to the same reality: God is not asking us to have everything figured out. He is asking us to step into the light and allow Him to guide us. And the very act of wrestling with these readings—questioning our motives, our desires, and the pull of our ego—is often the first sign that we are beginning to wake up.
